card.name: Dutty Wine
card.tagline: A high-intensity Jamaican dancehall move marked by rapid neck rotation and hip gyration.
card.profile: The Dutty Wine is a Jamaican dancehall style created in the early 2000s and popularized globally around 2006. Typically performed by women, it combines intense neck rotations with simultaneous wrist turning, hip winding, and low leg movements. While popularized by Tony Matterhorn's hit song of the same name, creators such as Mad Michelle and Montego Bay's The Attitude Girls pioneered its core physical expression. Due to its forceful cervical rotation, medical professionals have raised warnings regarding muscle trauma and neck strain.
card.insight: In 2006, Jamaican artist Tony Matterhorn propelled the Dutty Wine into a global phenomenon, where dancers like Shalara Gayle performed its dramatic, neck-rotating movements at extreme speeds.

card.profile_long:
ORIGINS AND HISTORY
The Dutty Wine originated in Jamaica alongside iconic dancehall creations such as 'Log on' and 'Screechie'. While several dancers claimed origin, dancehall queen Mad Michelle traced her performance of the move to a 2003 video recording. However, the packaged visual concept of the dance emerged strongly from a Montego Bay dance group named The Attitude Girls. Dancehall Queen Shalara Gayle, a prominent member of The Attitude Girls, became famous for executing the fastest and longest Dutty Wine routine. The movement erupted into a global craze in 2006 after dancehall artist Tony Matterhorn released his number-one single 'Dutty Wine', recorded on the Smash riddim. Following this release, the dance spread rapidly throughout international dancehall communities, particularly across parts of the United Kingdom and North America.

HOW IT IS DANCED
The core kinetic component of the Dutty Wine involves continuous, fluid gyration, often referred to in dancehall culture as 'winding'. The dancer initiates a rapid rotating movement of the neck, swinging their head in rhythm with the music. Simultaneously, the dancer coordinates bird-like leg movements alongside continuous rotations of the wrists, neck, and posterior. Dancers adjust their spatial posture depending on difficulty, dropping into lower stances to emphasize waist control. Advanced practitioners elevate the physical challenge by dropping into full splits while keeping the neck and posterior rotation active. Beginners typically start by isolating the hip and wrist rotations before introducing the controlled circular neck movement to ensure rhythm and balance.

MUSIC AND INSTRUMENTS
Music for the Dutty Wine is grounded in contemporary Jamaican dancehall, driven by digital riddims designed for modern club and sound system culture. The definitive musical backing of the movement is Tony Matterhorn's 2006 track 'Dutty Wine', composed over the high-tempo Smash riddim. The music features driving basslines, syncopated electronic drum patterns, and vocal calls tailored to lead the dancer's tempo and energetic physical execution.

COSTUME AND SETTING
The Dutty Wine is rooted in Jamaican dancehall spaces, night sessions, stage competitions, and global urban club culture. Dancers traditionally perform in vibrant dancehall fashion, often choosing outfits that highlight fluid body isolations, waist dynamics, and expressive physical performance during high-energy dancehall sessions.

OCCASIONS AND MEANING
Executed primarily during dancehall sessions, street parties, and international Dancehall Queen competitions, the Dutty Wine represents female athletic virtuosity, physical stamina, and personal flair within dancehall culture. The move allows dancers to display technical speed, muscular control, and rhythmic dexterity within an intensely competitive performance setting.

NOTABLE FIGURES
Key historical figures associated with the dance include Mad Michelle, a dancehall queen who documented early performances of the move in 2003. The dance trio The Attitude Girls from Montego Bay consolidated the performance concept, with group member Dancehall Queen Shalara Gayle renowned for performing the fastest and longest iterations of the dance. Musically, dancehall artist Tony Matterhorn anchored the movement within global popular culture through his chart-topping 2006 track.

REGIONAL VARIANTS
Following its 2006 global surge, the Dutty Wine developed regional presence within Caribbean diaspora communities across North America and the United Kingdom. While the foundational elements of neck rotation, wrist turning, and posterior gyration remained consistent, local dancehall groups adapted the move into stage routines and crew performance showcases.

LINEAGE
The Dutty Wine belongs to the modern lineage of Jamaican dancehall moves created in urban community contexts alongside moves like 'Log on' and 'Screechie'. It reflects the evolution of female dancehall movement styles, blending dynamic isolations with competitive performance traditions.

basic_steps: Isolate waist and execute fluid circular posterior gyration ('wine')
Rotate wrists simultaneously in rhythm with hip movement
Step feet in rhythmic bird-like leg movements
Incorporate controlled continuous circular rotation of the neck
Advanced option: drop down into splits while maintaining neck and posterior rotations
teaching.rhythm: Up-tempo 4/4 syncopated dancehall riddim (Smash riddim beat)
teaching.formation: Solo, small group, or competitive circle showcase
teaching.level_notes: Beginners must master neck and waist isolations separately before integrating rapid head rotations due to physical strain risks.

claims.text: The Dutty Wine is a Jamaican dance performed typically by young women.
The dance originated in Jamaica along with other dances such as Log on and Screechie.
Dancehall queen Mad Michelle refers to a 2003 video recording as evidence of creating the dance.
The packaged concept of the Dutty Wine came from a Montego Bay trio named The Attitude Girls.
Dancehall Queen Shalara Gayle of The Attitude Girls is famous for doing the fastest and longest Dutty Wine dance.
The dance was popularized in 2006 by Tony Matterhorn's song of the same name on the Smash riddim.
The dance involves rotating movement of the neck alongside leg, wrist, and posterior movements.
Doctors have warned that performing the Dutty Wine may cause serious muscle trauma, ligament damage, and neck injury.

signature_moves.name: Neck Rotation
signature_moves.description: Continuous circular motion of the neck and head in rhythm with the music.

signature_moves.name: Dutty Wine Splits
signature_moves.description: Dropping into full splits while maintaining posterior and head gyration.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Low ground levels including squats and full splits; no high vertical jumps.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid uncontrolled or jerky neck twisting; medical professionals warn of potential muscle trauma and ligament damage to the neck.
